## Overview

The Garo are a Tibeto-Burman ethnic group living mainly in Meghalaya in Northeast India, especially across the Garo Hills, with smaller communities in Assam, Tripura, West Bengal, Nagaland, and Bangladesh. They are also found in the Mymensingh Division, including Jamalpur, Sherpur, and Mymensingh districts, and in Dhaka. The Garo population across Meghalaya, Assam, Nagaland, Tripura, West Bengal, Canada, the US, Europe, Australia, and Bangladesh is estimated at more than 1 million. Garo is a Tibeto-Burman language, also described as belonging to the Baric group of the Sino-Tibetan family. Garo culture includes matrilineal social organization, agricultural festivals, distinctive clothing and ornaments, traditional weapons, rice-based foodways, and the Songsarek religious tradition.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

The sources name clothing and ornament traditions.

**Dakmanda** — A traditional dress of Garo women.

**Dakshari** — Another traditional dress of Garo women.

**Eking** — A small cloth worn around the waist by women in remote villages in the Garo Hills.

### Clothing & dress

Garo women traditionally wear *Dakmanda* and *Dakshari*. Women in remote villages in the Garo Hills wear an *eking*, described as a small cloth worn around the waist. Contemporary clothing includes jeans, sari, T-shirts, and pajamas for women, while Garo men wear jeans, T-shirts, and shirts. Clothing is also part of public festival performance: at the Dhaka Wangala, participants gather in traditional dress, while the Asanang Wangala includes women’s colourful costumes during dancing.

### Architecture

The sources mention the Nokpante, the village bachelor dormitory where unmarried male youths traditionally live.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They do document metalwork in weapons and ornaments. The *mil·am* is a two-edged sword made from a single piece of iron from hilt to point, with a cross-bar between the hilt and blade carrying a bunch of ox’s tail hair. Other weapons include shields, spears, bows and arrows, axes, and daggers. Brass is used for several ornaments, including ear rings, bangles, necklaces, and elbow rings.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Garo men and women wear a range of ornaments. *Nadongbi* or *sisa* is a brass ring worn in the lobe of the ear, while *Nadirong* is a brass ring worn in the upper part of the ear. *Natapsi* is a string of beads worn in the upper part of the ear. *Jaksan* refers to bangles of different materials and sizes. *Ripok* are necklaces made from long barrel-shaped beads of cornelian or red glass; others are made from brass or silver and worn on special occasions. *Jaksil* is an elbow ring worn by rich men at Gana ceremonies. Women’s ornaments include *Penta*, a small piece of ivory projecting upwards from the upper ear, *Seng·ki*, a waistband consisting of several rows of conch shells, and *Pilne*, a head ornament worn during dances.

## Music & performance

The sources describe music mainly in connection with Wangala festivals. At the Asanang Wangala, Garo boys called *pante* beat a long drum called *dama* in groups and play bamboo flutes. Garo girls, called *nomil*, dance in colourful costumes to the sound of the *dama* and folk songs. The festival is also called the “100-drum festival.”

Drum performances are central to the Dhaka Wangala, which includes an energetic rally, traditional dress, and speeches by special guests. The festival also features displays of traditional food, dress, and other materials.

The sources also describe the Simsang Festival, first started in 2006 in Williamnagar, Meghalaya. Formerly known as the Winter festival, it promotes local bands, exhibitions of handicrafts made by local people, and indigenous games of the Garo.

## Dance & theatre

The sources document communal dancing during Wangala festivals. At Asanang, Garo girls called *nomil* dance in a circle to the sound of the *dama* and folk songs, while boys called *pante* perform with drums and bamboo flutes. The Dhaka Wangala includes public celebration, traditional dress, and drum performances. No Garo theatre, mask tradition, shadow-puppet tradition, or named dramatic genre is described in the sources.

## Festivals & rituals

Garo festivals are generally connected with the agricultural cycle. The largest celebration is **Wangala**, the harvest festival held in October or November every year. It is a thanksgiving after the harvest in honour of Saljong, described as the provider of nature’s bounties.

The **Asanang Wangala**, also called the “100-drum festival,” is held in Asanang near Tura in the West Garo Hills, Meghalaya, India, usually in October or November. Thousands of people gather there, especially young people. Boys called *pante* perform with *dama* drums and bamboo flutes, while girls called *nomil* dance in a circle.

The **Dhaka Wangala** is held every year, usually in November or December, at the Lalmatia Housing Society ground. It includes a rally, drum performances, traditional dress, speeches, display stalls, traditional food, and other materials associated with Garo culture.

Other named festivals include **Gal·mak Goa** and **Agalmaka**. The **Simsang Festival** began in 2006 in Williamnagar and was formerly known as the Winter festival. The **Ahaia Winter Festival**, conceptualised in 2008, is a three-day event including cultural shows, food festivals, ethnic-wear competitions, exhibitions, and games.

Christmas is also a major season of celebration in the Garo Hills. In December, Tura and other towns are illuminated with lights, and worship, dancing, feasting, and social visits continue until 10 January.

## Foodways

Rice is the staple Garo food. Kochu, meaning taro, millet, maize, and tapioca are important substitutes when rice is scarce. Other popular foods include dried fish, bamboo shoots, sorrell, sweet potato, pumpkin, gourd, and banana.

Garo cooking traditionally uses a kind of potash made by burning dry pieces of plantain stems or young bamboo. This material is known locally as *kalchi* or *katchi*. The ashes are collected, dipped in water, and strained into conical shapes through a bamboo strainer. Cooking soda has become a more common replacement for this ash water.

Garo people ferment a special kind of rice to produce a liquor called *Minil Bichi*. This country liquor has an important place in Garo life. *Chu* is described as the sacred drink of the Garos. Garo children are given it at birth, and visiting guests are traditionally offered it. Festival display stalls may include traditional food, particularly during the Dhaka Wangala.

## Oral tradition & literature

Garo oral tradition recounts a migration from Tibet, referred to as *Tibotgre*, around 400 BC under the leadership of Jappa Jalimpa, Sukpa, and Bongepa. The migrants crossed the Brahmaputra River, called *Songdu Chibima*, temporarily settled in the river valley, and later established themselves in the Garo Hills.

The sources also mention oral narratives and transformational myths in the title of a later study concerning the Garo community of Tripura and Assam. Written records of the Garo date from around 1800. Two early histories are Major A. Playfair’s *The Garos*, published in 1909, and Sinha T.C.’s *The Psyche of Garos*, published in 1955.

Preservation efforts include the organization **Risi Jilma**, founded in 2000 to safeguard the ancient Garo Songsarek religion. The group became active in about 480 villages in and around the Garo Hills as the Songsarek population declined.

## Language & religion

Garo belongs to the Tibeto-Burman language family and to the Baric group of the Sino-Tibetan family. It is spoken in Meghalaya, Assam, Tripura, and areas of Bangladesh. Named dialects include *A·we*, *Am·beng* or *A·beng*, *Matabeng*, *Atong*, *Me·gam*, *Matchi*, *Dual*, *Ruga*, *Chibok*, *Chisak*, and *Gara Ganching*. Garo acquired a Latin-based writing system through American Baptist missionaries; the Latin alphabet completely replaced the Bengali script by 1924. The language is also sometimes written in the *A·chik Tokbirim* script, invented in 1979 by Arun Richil Marak.

Most Garos in India follow Christianity, while a smaller number practice the traditional Garo animist religion, Songsarek. Songsarek includes deities appeased through rituals, ceremonies, and animal sacrifices for the welfare of the tribe. In Bangladesh, Christianity and Songsarek are both practiced, and a small percentage of the Garo population in India practices Buddhism.
